newsitem.title: ITALY: Analysts confirm Italy Nov CPI forecast at 2.6 pct.
newsitem.headline: Analysts confirm Italy Nov CPI forecast at 2.6 pct.

text.p: Italy's November year-on-year inflation rate was seen at 2.6 percent after data from the last four of 10 Italian sample cities, analysts said.
Turin, Venice, Naples and Florence announced their consumer price data on Friday after the other six cities announced their figures on Thursday.
A Reuter poll of 12 economists earlier this week had forecast that November inflation should continue falling to 2.6 percent year-on-year after a 3.0 percent annual rate in October.
On Thursday, analysts said preliminary data from Milan, Genoa, Trieste, Bologna, Perugia and Naples had indicated a year-on-year rate for November of 2.6 percent.
The 10 sample cities have a combined weighting of 69.67 percent on the total index.
National statistics institute Istat will publish the final official figure on December 5.

Ilaria Fornari, analyst with JP Morgan in Milan, said that while she forecasts a November rate of 2.6 percent, she said "a final figure for November of 2.5 percent cannot be excluded. A good figure from Rome, which is not included in the sample cities, could round the rate down to 2.5."
Marcello Esposito of Banca Commerciale Italiana took more or less the same line. "There's a 66 percent possibility that November CPI will be 2.6 percent," he said.

Fornari noted that for a rounding down to an annual 2.5-percent monthly rise of less than 0.23 percent from cities not included in the sample 10 would be necessary, as against a monthly rise of 0.27 percent posted by the 10 cities.
Martino Dolfini of Chase Manhattan Bank forecast a month-on-month rise in November of 0.3 percent, giving a yearly 2.6 percent rate.

Lorenzo Codogno of Bank of America here also saw a 2.6-percent rate. "The situation is not as good as we might have expected after Thursday's figures, but it is still a good figure and one which could justify a Bank of Italy interest rate cut, he said.

"No one would be surprised if the central bank cut its 7.5 percent discount rate later today. But with Bank governor Antonio Fazio abroad (at a European banking congress in Frankfurt), there's a slight practical problem and of course, the Bank might prefer to first see market reaction to the lira's return to ther European exchange rate mechanism," Esposito said.
